questions.a: After the consecration, there is no longer either bread or wine, but only the species or appearances remain, without the substance.

questions.q: What are the species or appearances?
questions.a: The species or appearances are all that falls under the senses, such as the figure, the color, the odor, and the taste of bread and wine.

questions.q: Under the appearances of bread is there only the Body of Jesus Christ, or under those of wine only His Blood?
questions.a: No: under the appearances of bread is the whole Jesus Christ, in Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity; and so also under those of wine.

questions.q: When the host is broken into many parts, is the Body of Jesus Christ broken?
questions.a: When the host is broken into many parts, the Body of Jesus Christ is not broken, but only the species of bread; and the Body of the Lord remains whole in each part.

questions.q: Is Jesus Christ found in all the consecrated hosts of the world?
questions.a: Yes, Jesus Christ is found in all the consecrated hosts of the world.

questions.q: Why is the Most Holy Eucharist preserved in churches?
questions.a: The Most Holy Eucharist is preserved in churches so that the faithful may adore it, may receive it in Communion, and may sense in it the perpetual assistance and presence of Jesus Christ in the Church. § 3. Holy Communion: Dispositions, Obligation, Effects

questions.q: How many things are necessary to make a good Communion?
questions.a: To make a good Communion three things are necessary: 1. to be in the grace of God; 2. to know and to think about whom one is going to receive; 3. to be fasting from midnight.

questions.q: What does "to be in the grace of God" mean?
questions.a: To be in the grace of God means to have one's conscience clean of every mortal sin.

questions.q: Does one who receives Communion knowing that he is in mortal sin receive Jesus Christ?
questions.a: One who receives Communion knowing that he is in mortal sin does receive Jesus Christ, but not His grace; rather, by committing a horrible sacrilege, he renders himself deserving of damnation.

questions.q: What does "to know and to think about whom one is going to receive" mean?
questions.a: To know and to think about whom one is going to receive means to approach Our Lord Jesus Christ in the Eucharist with living faith, with ardent desire, and with deep humility and modesty.

questions.q: What fast is required before Communion?
questions.a: Before Communion the natural — that is, total — fast is required, which is broken by anything taken in the manner of food or drink.

questions.q: Is Communion ever permitted to one who is not fasting?
questions.a: Communion is permitted to one who is not fasting in danger of death, and during long illnesses, under the conditions determined by the Church.

questions.q: Is there an obligation to receive Communion?
questions.a: There is an obligation to receive Communion every year at Easter, and in danger of death, as Viaticum, to sustain the soul on its journey to eternity.

questions.q: At what age does the obligation of the Easter Communion begin?
questions.a: The obligation of the Easter Communion begins at the age at which one is capable of making it with sufficient dispositions, that is, ordinarily about the seventh year.

questions.q: Is it good and useful to receive Communion often?
questions.a: It is most good and most useful to receive Communion often, even every day, provided one always does so with the proper dispositions.

questions.q: After Communion, how long does Jesus Christ remain in us?
questions.a: After Communion, Jesus Christ remains in us as long as the eucharistic species last.

questions.q: What effects does the Eucharist produce in one who receives it worthily?
questions.a: The Eucharist, in one who receives it worthily, preserves and increases the grace that is the life of the soul, as food does for the life of the body; remits venial sins and preserves from mortal ones; gives spiritual consolation and comfort, increasing charity and the hope of eternal life, of which it is the pledge.

questions.q: Is the Eucharist only a sacrament?
questions.a: The Eucharist is not only a sacrament, but is also the permanent sacrifice of the New Testament, and as such is called the Holy Mass.

questions.q: What is sacrifice?
questions.a: Sacrifice is the public offering to God of a thing that is destroyed in order to profess that He is the Creator and supreme Master, to whom everything entirely is due.

questions.q: What is the Holy Mass?
questions.a: The Holy Mass is the sacrifice of the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ which, under the species of bread and wine, is offered by the priest to God upon the altar, in memory and renewal of the sacrifice of the Cross.

questions.q: Is the sacrifice of the Mass the same sacrifice as that of the Cross?
questions.a: The sacrifice of the Mass is the same sacrifice as that of the Cross; there is only a difference in the manner of accomplishing it.

questions.q: What difference is there between the sacrifice of the Cross and that of the Mass?
questions.a: Between the sacrifice of the Cross and that of the Mass there is this difference: that Jesus Christ on the Cross sacrificed Himself by voluntarily giving His own Blood, and merited every grace for us; whereas on the altar He, without shedding blood, sacrifices and annihilates Himself mystically through the ministry of the priest, and applies to us the merits of the sacrifice of the Cross.

questions.q: For what ends is the Mass offered to God?
questions.a: The Mass is offered to God in order to render Him supreme worship of latria or adoration, to thank Him for His benefits, to appease Him and to give Him satisfaction for our sins, and to obtain graces for the benefit of the faithful living and departed.

questions.q: Is the Mass not also offered to the Saints?
questions.a: The Mass is not offered to the Saints, but to God alone, even when it is celebrated in honor of the Saints: sacrifice belongs only to the Creator and supreme Master.

questions.q: Are we bound to hear Mass?
questions.a: We are bound to hear Mass on Sundays and on the other commanded feast days; but it is profitable to assist at it often, in order to share in the greatest act of religion, supremely pleasing to God and meritorious.

questions.q: What is the most fitting way to assist at Mass?
questions.a: The most fitting way to assist at Mass is to offer it to God in union with the priest, recalling the sacrifice of the Cross — that is, the Passion and Death of the Lord — and receiving Communion: Communion is real union with the immolated Victim, and is therefore the greatest sharing in the Holy Sacrifice.

questions.q: What is Penance?
questions.a: Penance, or Confession, is the sacrament instituted by Jesus Christ to forgive the sins committed after Baptism.

questions.q: When was the sacrament of Penance instituted by Jesus Christ?
questions.a: The sacrament of Penance was instituted by Jesus Christ when He said to the Apostles, and in them to their successors: "Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained" (John XX. 22-23).

questions.q: Who is the minister of Penance?
questions.a: The minister of Penance is the priest approved by the Bishop.

questions.q: How many and what things are required to make a good confession?
questions.a: To make a good confession five things are required: 1. the examination of conscience; 2. sorrow for sins; 3. the resolution to commit them no more; 4. the confession; 5. satisfaction or penance.

questions.q: How is the examination of conscience made?
questions.a: The examination of conscience is made by recalling to mind the sins committed in thoughts, words, deeds, and omissions, against the commandments of God, the precepts of the Church, and the obligations of one's state in life, beginning from the last well-made confession.

questions.q: In the examination must we seek out the number of our sins?
questions.a: In the examination we must diligently seek out also the number of our mortal sins.

questions.q: What is sorrow?
questions.a: Sorrow, or repentance, is that displeasure with and hatred of the sins committed which makes us resolve not to sin again.

questions.q: How many kinds of sorrow are there?
questions.a: Sorrow is of two kinds: perfect, or contrition; and imperfect, or attrition.

questions.q: What is perfect sorrow, or contrition?
questions.a: Perfect sorrow, or contrition, is the displeasure for the sins committed because they are an offense against God our Father, infinitely good and lovable, and the cause of the Passion and Death of Our Redeemer Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

questions.q: Why is contrition perfect sorrow?
questions.a: Contrition is perfect sorrow because it springs from a perfect motive — the filial love of God, or charity — and because it obtains for us at once the forgiveness of sins, although the obligation of confessing them remains.

questions.q: What is imperfect sorrow, or attrition?
questions.a: Imperfect sorrow, or attrition, is the displeasure for the sins committed, out of fear of eternal and temporal punishments, or also because of the ugliness of sin.

questions.q: Why is attrition imperfect sorrow?
questions.a: Attrition is imperfect sorrow because it springs from less perfect motives — those proper to servants rather than to children — and because it does not obtain for us the forgiveness of sins except through the sacrament.

questions.q: Is it necessary to have sorrow for all the sins committed?
questions.a: It is necessary to have sorrow for all the mortal sins committed, without exception; and it is fitting to have sorrow also for the venial ones.

questions.q: Why is it necessary to have sorrow for all mortal sins?
questions.a: It is necessary to have sorrow for all mortal sins because by any one of them we have gravely offended God, lost His grace, and merited to remain separated from Him forever.

questions.q: What is the resolution?
questions.a: The resolution is the firm will never again to commit sins and to flee their occasions.

questions.q: What is the occasion of sin?
questions.a: The occasion of sin is whatever puts us in danger of sinning, whether a person or a thing.

questions.q: Are we bound to flee the occasions of sins?
questions.a: We are bound to flee the occasions of sins, because we are bound to flee sin: whoever does not flee them ends by falling, since "he who loves danger will perish in it" (Ecclus. III. 27).

questions.q: What is confession?
questions.a: Confession is the accusation of one's sins made to the priest confessor, in order to receive absolution.

questions.q: Of what sins are we bound to confess?
questions.a: We are bound to confess all mortal sins not yet confessed, or confessed badly; but it is profitable to confess venial sins also.

questions.q: How must we accuse our mortal sins?
questions.a: We must accuse our mortal sins fully, without letting ourselves be overcome by a false shame to keep any silent, declaring their kind, their number, and also the circumstances that would add a new grave malice.

questions.q: What must one do who does not remember the precise number of his mortal sins?
questions.a: One who does not remember the precise number of his mortal sins must indicate the number that seems to him closest to the truth.

questions.q: Why must we not let ourselves be overcome by shame to keep silent some mortal sin?
questions.a: We must not let ourselves be overcome by shame to keep silent some mortal sin, because we confess to Jesus Christ in the person of the confessor, and the confessor cannot reveal any sin, even at the cost of his life; and because, otherwise, not obtaining forgiveness, we shall be put to shame before all at the universal judgment.

questions.q: Would one who through shame or some other motive kept silent a mortal sin make a good confession?
questions.a: One who through shame or any other unjust motive kept silent a mortal sin would not make a good confession, but would commit a sacrilege.

questions.q: What must one do who knows he has not confessed well?
questions.a: One who knows he has not confessed well must repeat the badly made confessions and accuse himself of the sacrileges committed.

questions.q: Has one made a good confession who without fault left out or forgot a mortal sin?
questions.a: One who without fault left out or forgot a mortal sin has made a good confession; but the obligation remains for him to accuse himself of it afterward. § 4. Absolution — Satisfaction — Indulgences

questions.q: What is absolution?
questions.a: Absolution is the sentence by which the priest, in the name of Jesus Christ, forgives the penitent's sins, saying: "I absolve you from your sins, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen."

questions.q: When sins are forgiven by absolution, is also every punishment merited forgiven?
questions.a: When sins are forgiven by absolution, the eternal punishment merited by mortal sin is forgiven; but unless one has the most perfect contrition, there ordinarily remains, to be paid in this life or in the next, a temporal punishment.

questions.q: What is satisfaction, or sacramental penance?
questions.a: Satisfaction, or sacramental penance, is the good work imposed by the confessor as a chastisement and correction of the sinner, and to pay off the temporal punishment merited by sinning.

questions.q: When is it fitting to perform sacramental penance?
questions.a: It is fitting to perform sacramental penance as soon as possible, if the confessor has not assigned a specific time for it.

questions.q: Does sacramental penance suffice to free us from all the temporal punishment merited by sin?
questions.a: Sacramental penance does not, ordinarily, suffice to free us from all the temporal punishment merited by sin; and therefore it is fitting to make up for it by other works of penance and piety, and by indulgences.

questions.q: What are the works of penance and of piety?
questions.a: The works of penance and of piety are: fasting, mortifications, the acts of spiritual and corporal mercy, prayers, and the devout use of those blessed things and those sacred ceremonies which are called sacramentals, such as holy water and the various blessings. 385 a. The seven corporal works of mercy: 1. To feed the hungry; 2. To give drink to the thirsty; 3. To clothe the naked; 4. To shelter the homeless; 5. To visit the sick; 6. To visit the imprisoned; 7. To bury the dead. 385 b. The seven spiritual works of mercy: 1. To counsel the doubtful; 2. To instruct the ignorant; 3. To admonish sinners; 4. To comfort the afflicted; 5. To forgive offences; 6. To bear wrongs patiently; 7. To pray for the living and the dead.

questions.q: What is an indulgence?
questions.a: An indulgence is a remission of the temporal punishment due for sins, which the Church grants under certain conditions to one who is in grace, by applying to him the superabundant merits and satisfactions of Jesus Christ, of Our Lady, and of the Saints, which constitute the treasury of the Church.

questions.q: How many kinds of indulgence are there?
questions.a: Indulgence is of two kinds: plenary and partial.

questions.q: What is the plenary indulgence?
questions.a: The plenary indulgence is the one that remits all the temporal punishment due for sins.

questions.q: What is the partial indulgence?
questions.a: The partial indulgence is the one that remits only a part of the temporal punishment due for sins.

questions.q: What is meant by an indulgence of "forty" or "a hundred days," of "seven years," and the like?
questions.a: By an indulgence of forty or a hundred days, of seven years, and the like, is meant the remission of as much temporal punishment as would have been paid off by forty days, a hundred days, or seven years of the penance anciently established by the Church.

questions.q: What is required to gain indulgences?
questions.a: To gain indulgences it is required to be in the state of grace and to perform well the prescribed works.

questions.q: What is Extreme Unction?
questions.a: Extreme Unction, also called Holy Oil, is the sacrament instituted for the spiritual — and also bodily — relief of Christians who are gravely ill.

questions.q: Who is the minister of Extreme Unction?
questions.a: The minister of Extreme Unction is the parish priest, or another priest who has permission for it.

questions.q: How does the priest administer Extreme Unction?
questions.a: The priest administers Extreme Unction by anointing in the form of a cross, with oil blessed by the Bishop, the organs of the senses of the sick person, saying: "By this holy anointing and by His most loving mercy, may the Lord forgive you every fault committed by sight, by hearing, etc. Amen."

questions.q: What effects does Extreme Unction produce?
questions.a: Extreme Unction increases sanctifying grace; it blots out venial sins, and even mortal sins that the sick person, being only attrite, cannot confess; it gives strength to bear illness patiently, to resist temptations, and to die a holy death; and it also helps to restore health, if it is good for the soul.

questions.q: When can Holy Oil be given?
questions.a: Holy Oil can be given when the illness is dangerous; and it is good to give it immediately after confession and Viaticum, while the sick person retains his awareness.

questions.q: What is "Holy Orders"?
questions.a: Holy Orders is the sacrament that gives the power to perform the sacred actions concerning the Eucharist and the salvation of souls, and imprints the character of ministers of God.

questions.q: Who is the minister of Holy Orders?
questions.a: The minister of Holy Orders is the Bishop, who gives the Holy Spirit and the sacred power by imposing his hands and handing over the sacred objects proper to the Order, while pronouncing the words of the prescribed form.

questions.q: Why is the sacrament that makes the ministers of God called Order?
questions.a: The sacrament that makes the ministers of God is called Order because it includes various grades of ministers, one subordinate to another, from which results the sacred Hierarchy.

questions.q: What are the grades of the sacred Hierarchy?
questions.a: The grades of the sacred Hierarchy are: the minor Orders, the Subdiaconate, and the Diaconate, which are preparatory; the Presbyterate or Priesthood, which gives the power to consecrate the Eucharist and to forgive sins; and the Episcopate, the fullness of the Priesthood, which gives the power to confer Orders and to teach and govern the faithful.

questions.q: Is the dignity of the Priesthood great?
questions.a: The dignity of the Priesthood is most great, because of its power over the real Body of Jesus Christ, which it makes present in the Eucharist, and over His mystical body, the Church, which it governs, with the sublime mission of leading men to holiness and to the blessed life.

questions.q: What end must one who enters Holy Orders have?
questions.a: One who enters Holy Orders must have for his end solely the glory of God and the salvation of souls.

questions.q: Can anyone enter Holy Orders of his own choice?
questions.a: No one can enter Holy Orders of his own choice, but must be called by God through his own Bishop; that is, he must have the vocation, with the virtues and the aptitudes for the sacred ministry that the vocation requires.

questions.q: Would one who entered the Priesthood without a vocation do wrong?
questions.a: One who entered the Priesthood without a vocation would do very wrong, because he could only with difficulty observe its most exalted duties, with evident danger of public scandal and of eternal perdition.

questions.q: What duties have the faithful toward those called to Holy Orders?
questions.a: The faithful have the duty of leaving to their children and dependents full freedom to follow their vocation; also of asking God for good pastors and ministers, and of fasting for this end on the four Ember Days; finally, of venerating the ordained as persons consecrated to God.

questions.q: What is Matrimony?
questions.a: Matrimony is the sacrament that unites man and woman indissolubly, as Jesus Christ and the Church His spouse are united, and gives them the grace to live together in holiness and to raise their children in a Christian way.

questions.q: Who is the minister of Matrimony?
questions.a: The ministers of Matrimony are the spouses who contract it.

questions.q: How is Matrimony contracted?
questions.a: Matrimony is contracted by expressing the mutual consent before the parish priest, or a priest delegated by him, and at least two witnesses.

questions.q: Does Matrimony celebrated in this form also obtain civil effects in Italy?
questions.a: Matrimony celebrated in this form also obtains civil effects in Italy, because the Italian State recognizes such effects in the Sacrament of Matrimony.

questions.q: How does Matrimony so celebrated obtain civil effects in Italy?
questions.a: Matrimony so celebrated obtains civil effects in Italy through its regular transcription in the registers of the civil state, made at the request of the parish priest.

questions.q: Can Catholic spouses also perform a civil marriage?
questions.a: Catholic spouses cannot perform a civil marriage either before or after the religious Matrimony; should they dare to do so even with the intention of celebrating the religious Matrimony afterward, they are considered by the Church to be public sinners.

questions.q: Must the spouses be in the grace of God when contracting Matrimony?
questions.a: The spouses must be in the grace of God when contracting Matrimony; otherwise they commit a sacrilege.

questions.q: What duties have the spouses?
questions.a: The spouses have the duty to live together in holiness, to help one another with constant affection in their spiritual and temporal needs, and to raise their children well, caring for their soul no less than for their body, and forming them above all in religion and in virtue by word and by example.

questions.q: What is prayer?
questions.a: Prayer is a pious raising of the soul to God in order to know Him well, to adore Him, to thank Him, and to ask Him for what we need.

questions.q: How many kinds of prayer are there?
questions.a: There are two kinds of prayer: mental and vocal.

questions.q: What is mental prayer?
questions.a: Mental prayer is that which is made with the mind and the heart alone: such are the meditation of the Christian truths, and contemplation.

questions.q: What is vocal prayer?
questions.a: Vocal prayer, more commonly called simply "prayer," is that which is made with words accompanied by the mind and the heart.

questions.q: How must we pray?
questions.a: We must pray reflecting that we are in the presence of the infinite majesty of God, and that we are in need of His mercy; and therefore we must be humble, attentive, and devout.

questions.q: Is it necessary to pray?
questions.a: It is necessary to pray, and to pray often, because God commands it; and ordinarily it is only when one prays that He grants spiritual and temporal graces.

questions.q: Why does God grant the graces we ask of Him?
questions.a: God grants the graces we ask of Him because He, who is most faithful, has promised to hear us if we pray with confidence and perseverance in the name of Jesus Christ.

questions.q: Why must we pray to God in the name of Jesus Christ?
questions.a: We must pray to God in the name of Jesus Christ, because only through Him, His Son and the one Mediator between God and men, do our prayers and good works have value; for this reason the Church is accustomed to end her prayers with these or equivalent words: "through your Son Jesus Christ, Our Lord."

questions.q: Why are we not always heard in our prayers?
questions.a: We are not always heard in our prayers either because we pray badly, or because we ask for things not useful to our true good, that is, to our spiritual good.

questions.q: What things must we ask of God?
questions.a: We must ask of God His glory, and for ourselves eternal life and even temporal graces, as Jesus Christ has taught us in the Our Father.

questions.q: What is the Our Father?
questions.a: The Our Father is the prayer taught and recommended by Jesus Christ; it is therefore called the Lord's Prayer, and it is the most excellent of all prayers.

questions.q: Why is the Our Father the most excellent prayer?
questions.a: The Our Father is the most excellent prayer because it came forth from the mind and Heart of Jesus, and contains in seven brief petitions all that we must ask of God as His children and as brothers among ourselves.

questions.q: What must we ask as good children of God?
questions.a: As good children of God we must ask that throughout the world His name be known and honored, that His kingdom — the Church — be spread, and that His most holy will be fulfilled by all: this is what is asked in the first three petitions of the Our Father.

questions.q: As brothers among ourselves, what must we ask?
questions.a: As brothers among ourselves we must ask for bodily and spiritual nourishment, the forgiveness of sins, the defense from temptations, and the deliverance from evil: this is what is asked, for ourselves and for all human beings, in the last four petitions of the Our Father.

questions.q: Why does Jesus Christ have us call upon God as "Our Father"?
questions.a: Jesus Christ has us call upon God as "Our Father" to remind us that God is truly the Father of all, especially of us Christians who, in Baptism, were adopted by Him as His children; and to inspire in us a great love and confidence toward Him.

questions.q: If God hears one who prays well, why do we also call upon Our Lady, the Angels, and the Saints?
questions.a: We also call upon Our Lady, the Angels, and the Saints because, being dear to the Lord and merciful toward us, they may help us in our petitions by their powerful intercession.

questions.q: Why are the Angels, the Saints, and Our Lady powerful intercessors before God?
questions.a: The Angels and the Saints are powerful intercessors before God because they are His faithful servants, indeed His chosen friends; Our Lady is most powerful because she is the Mother of God and full of grace, and for this reason we call upon her so often, all the more since she was left to us as our Mother by Jesus Christ.

questions.q: With what prayer especially do we call upon Our Lady?
questions.a: We call upon Our Lady especially with the Hail Mary, or Angelic Salutation, so called because it begins with the greeting that the Archangel Gabriel made to her when announcing that she was chosen to be the Mother of God.

questions.q: What do we ask of Our Lady in the Hail Mary?
questions.a: In the Hail Mary we ask Our Lady for her motherly intercession for us in life and in death.

questions.q: Does the invocation of Our Lady and of the Saints not perhaps show distrust in Jesus Christ, the one Mediator, as if His merits were not enough to obtain graces for us?
questions.a: The invocation of Our Lady and of the Saints shows no distrust in Jesus Christ, the one Mediator; on the contrary, it shows a greater faith in His merits, so great and so efficacious that through them, and only through them, Our Lady and the Saints have from God grace, merits, and the power of intercession.
